The floor panels were perforated with a dot matrix of vents that regularly replace all the air in the clean room. Above our heads, where twenty miles of rails had been installed for automated wafer transport, was the orderly traffic of inhuman motion. Robotic claws whispered along branching tracks, clutching boxy carriers beneath them like prizes in an arcade game. Inside the carriers were the prized wafers. This system, Jack said, had replaced an old method in which a person pushed the wafers in a cart. The human work was less stressful now, a colleague added. He’d once visited a fab with a sign that read “If you bump this cart, your pay will be docked X percent.” The facility was so important, one employee later mentioned, that “we pray to the local gods for auspicious function.”Inside the halls, the overhead claws descended to insert wafers into one end of the machines and withdraw them from the other. The only visible evidence of a human hand was paper coverings, which had been taped on the machines to obscure their respective logos. Apparently, there are people who can eyeball an Nvidia Vera Rubin or an Apple M6 from the positioning of, say, a Canon FPA-5520iV LF in relation to a Surfscan SP5XP, and T.S.M.C. had mistaken me for one of them. The machines themselves were perhaps less important than the choreography of their administration. As Jun He, the vice-president, put it, “Our key comparative advantage is the management of complexity.”The next day, my guides and I visited AP7, a partially finished facility an hour or two south. The tropical sun was oppressive, but company representatives were prepared with orange parasols, each with a dedicated barcode. Despite slight delays—the excavation of the site had turned up some priceless Neolithic pottery, and the company also had to establish a protected sanctuary for the ring-necked pheasant—the first phase had risen out of an old sugarcane field in only eighteen months. A wiry, blunt thirty-one-year veteran deputy director named K. H. Cheng had come in with a team of shock troops to supervise.An employee puts on a bunny suit to enter an ASML clean room.Photograph by Aleksey Kondratyev for The New YorkerThe second phase would come online in four to six months. At the loading dock, deliveries arrived in trucks lined up in a queue that had been planned a year in advance. The tools, Cheng explained, were accompanied by vender emissaries who would stay to help for the year it took for T.S.M.C.’s technicians to understand them as well as, or better than, their makers. When I asked if this practice held for ASML’s machines, he sighed. “Those people are here all the time, because only ASML’s designers know everything,” he said. He held up his index finger: “The only exception!” The companies in the industry form a continuum. Just as it’s not always clear where Zeiss ends and ASML begins, the border between ASML and T.S.M.C. is fuzzy. The chipmaker’s relationships with customers are similarly interlaced and sensitive. Two weeks earlier, Cheng told me, he’d hosted representatives from Apple. He said, “I try not to show too much to a customer. I show them as little as possible, because they always want more control.”For T.S.M.C., a new fab isn’t just a giant, particle-free building with a twenty-billion-dollar price tag. It’s an additional node in a network that extends across space and time. AP7’s employees were camped out in temporary offices and bought snacks from a temporary 7-Eleven. Greater energy appeared to be diverted to a construction project across the street: another science-park high school, where the next generation would be educated to take over where the current one leaves off.In 2023, President Joe Biden opened his State of the Union address by declaring that an injury had been done to our national pride. “These chips were invented in America,” he said. “We lost our edge.” An injury had also been done to the price of refrigerators and sedans. The remedy, the President said, was that “we’re going to make sure the supply chain for America begins in America.” The CHIPS and Science Act appropriated fifty billion dollars for the reindustrialization of the country on the back of the semiconductor. The second-largest award went to T.S.M.C., to build out a satellite complex in Arizona.This was easier said than done. Unlike its kin in Taiwan, the T.S.M.C. fab in Phoenix took about four years to be completed. Permitting and regulations presented the usual challenges, but what seemed to slow down T.S.M.C. the most was that it couldn’t rely on the construction pipeline it had cultivated at home. The first time a new contractor works for T.S.M.C., it’s given a relatively simple assignment, like a utilities building. The contractor is evaluated according to a set of standardized criteria, and if it does well it graduates to the next level. Cheng, the veteran deputy director, told me, “We do not make bets, and we do not take risks.”The riskiest part, for a company with universally stringent expectations, was hiring. About half the initial workforce was sent over wholesale from Taiwan. During my visit, nobody wanted to be impolitic about the talents of my countrymen, but it was clear that they were dubious about our skill sets and work ethic.I met Renee Tseng, a young woman in casually elegant denim, who was part of the first wave of Taiwanese employees sent to set up the Arizona operations. She works in the Yield Enhancement Department: before a wafer is routed from one stage of the process to the next, it is scanned by an electron microscope and assessed by an A.I. model, and any detected anomalies pop up on her screen for evaluation. (The company’s usage of A.I. effectively requires that it buy back its chips at a retail markup.) She had no formal training; in college, she studied foreign languages. But she’s been doing the job for sixteen years, which means that she can immediately distinguish between the curve-shaped scratch made by one tool and the star-shaped scratch made by another. Some people, she said with a shrug, have no aptitude for it: “They all look the same.” Others learn the trade, she continued, but it wasn’t exactly something that could be taught explicitly. As with many aspects of semiconductor manufacturing, there was a tacit knowledge that could be absorbed only by becoming part of a community of experienced practitioners. Hopefully, in time, her American counterparts would get their reps in.Another tricky thing about the Arizona site was that it had been severed from its links to local merchants. On one of my fab tours, I’d seen employees push handcarts outfitted with special shock absorbers to protect components from vibrations. These, as far as Jack knew, were made by only one company, in Taiwan, and had to be shipped to the States. There was no clean-room laundry in Phoenix that met T.S.M.C.’s standards, so all the bunny suits were schlepped back and forth across the desert.The catch, in the American attempt to make chips at home rather than overseas, is that chips aren’t really made anywhere at all. A chip can cross international borders more than seventy times before it’s shipped to a customer. T.S.M.C.’s part begins with silicon wafers, but these have their own far-flung prehistory. Leading-edge semiconductor-grade polysilicon must be purified to “eleven nines” (99.999999999 per cent), which only a handful of specialized companies—based in Michigan, Germany, and Japan—are poised to do. These silicon chunks are melted in bespoke crucibles made of the world’s purest quartz, virtually all of which is mined from a solitary deposit in the mountains of North Carolina. This process, which generates perfectly crystalline silicon ingots to be sliced like fragile metallic salamis into thin wafers, is entrusted largely to one firm in Taiwan and two in Japan. Most of the steps along this chain are controlled by monopolies or duopolies. This isn’t because of market manipulation. It’s because each endeavor is so esoteric, so formidable, and so crucial that it makes sense for all the available expertise to be concentrated in one or two nexuses.Just as important as the firms themselves are the associations between them. Toward the end of the Second World War, as the Red Army approached, the Allied powers moved Zeiss—even then, its lenses were strategically important—from its historic home in Germany’s east to the other side of the country. Considered in isolation, the idea of securing some of T.S.M.C.’s operations out of harm’s way, in Phoenix, makes similar sense. Broadly speaking, however, it’s incoherent to consider any given chip-industry node in isolation. The semiconductor supply chain is a planetary superorganism with its own ecology. It’s not like a plant that can be casually repotted.Chips are products of an organizational culture—both within companies and between them—that encourages people to look beyond their own personal horizons. Jayson Stewart, a San Diego physicist who works on ASML’s light source, told me that the firm’s “time frames are very forward-looking. I’m somewhat young, and we’re talking about 2050, things to come that are likely past my retirement.” There are quite a lot of ASML employees, he continued, who measure their monastic tenure in decades. Some of them have sat in the same clean room in the same bunny suit working on the same little nozzle for fifteen years. He recalled, “When one guy retired, he said, ‘Take care of my ASML’—not ‘ASML’ but ‘my ASML.’ ” To Schafgans, the engineering executive, even this felt too limited: “I’m grateful to be part of the whole chain.” This might sound like brochure patter, but if so it’s not the self-promotion of an individual company but the gestalt of the entire industry.“It’s all vegan, except for some of it.”Cartoon by Bruce Eric KaplanWhen I spoke with Mike Schmidt, who ran the main Biden Administration team responsible for the implementation of the CHIPS Act, I expressed some skepticism about the idea that a domestic industry could be conjured ex nihilo in the Arizona desert. I mentioned the lack of a clean-room laundry, and he said, “I love that about the bunny suits! It just kind of goes to show how much the ecosystem matters, right? Part of it is that in order to do it you have to do it, and then it becomes self-reinforcing. Five years from now, someone will be making a killing with a clean-room-laundry business in Phoenix.” A plant or two in Arizona wasn’t the U.S.’s ultimate goal but, rather, an initial seed. In time, he hoped, the desert would bloom. This was, he said, “quite self-consciously a generational program.”The best Chinese A.I. models lag behind our own by only three to six months. The near-parity in technical capabilities means little, however, as long as we retain our prodigiously advantaged access to chips. China lacks the virtuosity of T.S.M.C.’s process engineering, and it cannot yet match the lithographic capacity of even ASML’s older technologies, let alone its EUV machine. The country will catch up eventually. The rationale for the current export-controls regime is that we might in the meantime build an insurmountable lead.The U.S. government has prohibited the sale of ASML’s flagship product in China, but it continues to export an earlier generation of its machines. The Trump Administration has expressed a strong preference for ASML to stop doing even this much. If the company chooses to obey, the Chinese might retaliate with the denial of crucial rare-earth metals.Europe does not like being caught in the middle. In one recent scenario, European researchers ran a thought experiment in which the Pentagon ultimately identifies the loss of control over ASML’s machines as “a threat comparable to the proliferation of nuclear weapons.” Washington might then try to impose a joint-governance structure that would effectively nationalize a foreign company. Over dinner, I asked Benschop, the ASML vice-president, about the company’s status as a “choke point.” He said, “When I learned that word, I thought, I don’t want to be choked.”There is no shortage of confident soothsaying about A.I. It will cure cancer; it will replace all jobs; it will transform the battlefield; it will guarantee our political dominance; it will usher in a golden age of superabundance; it will bring about our extinction. What such predictions have in common is an assumption that A.I. developers will enjoy ever-greater access to ever-better chips. That access might be undermined by China. This is a question of geopolitics, in the normal sense of the term. It might also be undermined by the exhaustion of Moore’s Law. This, too, might be construed as a question of geopolitics. Moore’s Law has survived only on the basis of unprecedented international confederation.When elected officials or pundits talk about chips, they sound like they could be talking about oil or any other strategic asset that can be extracted. When people who know a lot about chips talk about them, they sound like they are talking about sacramental totems. The first point they want to make is always the same; as Dylan Patel, who runs the research-and-consulting firm SemiAnalysis, told me, “The main thing people don’t understand is that semiconductors are the most complicated things people do.” The second point they make, before there is time to articulate an objection, is that everyone’s intuitive response is incorrect. Patel continued, “Rockets are simple.” Brinton Johns, an investor at N.Z.S. Capital, said, of making chips, “It’s just so much harder. Rockets are an amazing accomplishment, yes. We don’t have a rating scale for complexity, but rockets are maybe a five or a six.” His investing partner, Jon Bathgate, finished the thought: “Semiconductors are an eleven.”A silicon wafer printed with ASML’s EUV machine.Photograph by Alastair Philip Wiper for The New YorkerA closeup of a silicon wafer.Photograph by Alastair Philip Wiper for The New YorkerAnd yet we take it for granted that we can build them. We shouldn’t. The chief determinant of that unlikely success has been not individual genius in the lab, or individual prowess in the boardroom, but collective planning and coördination at a breathtaking scale. Globalization has become tainted in our eyes, as if it necessarily constitutes a zero-sum enterprise. And its mercenary form—which is also its most common form—has indeed inflicted harm. But the global semiconductor supply chain reflects an alternative pathway. It has united its participants in the pursuit of something profoundly difficult that could not have been achieved in the absence of intercontinental solidarity.In its most spiritual version, Moore’s Law projected that our power would routinely double. But this idea was not original to Gordon Moore. It was Henry Adams, in 1904, who first proposed what he called the Law of Acceleration. The world’s output of coal, he’d noticed, had roughly doubled each decade since 1840. Should this rate hold, he imagined, an American in the year 2000 would have “unlimited” power and “think in complexities unimaginable to an earlier mind.” He’d been famously converted by an experience at the Paris Exposition’s great gallery of machines, where he perceived the towering inventions “as a moral force, much as the early Christians felt the Cross.” This devotion had sustained the generations who built the great cathedral at Chartres. What they had accomplished in the name of the Virgin was now accomplished in the name of the Dynamo. But what Adams took as objects of devotion might better be described as occasions for it. They have given vast numbers of individual people, largely unknown to one another, reason to collaborate on a project that they would not live to see completed.Last year, I happened to be talking to a Dutch archeologist, Maikel Kuijpers, about Neolithic monuments. Stonehenge, he said, has frequently been investigated as a technological mystery. We look at the enormous rock slabs retrieved from far-off sites by archaic peoples and can’t help but suspect that these ancients availed themselves of some precocious technology lost to history—a present from aliens, perhaps. But we know how they built it, Kuijpers went on. There isn’t any mystery. They gathered as many people and animals as they could, and distributed ropes, and together they hauled those tremendous slabs a great distance. This didn’t diminish their achievement. It made it, if anything, even more sublime. ♦The doxing of Jane Doe and the fallout from the “Cornell Seven” rape case.“She Made Me Do It”: a famed equestrian instructor shot his most annoying student.Parents disagreed on whether to vaccinate their children. blocks.html_en: This strikes almost all of us as ridiculous. A microchip is a bauble of metal and refined sand. It doesn’t appear to have epic proportions. Upon close examination, however, the epic proportions are there in miniature. Imagine a perfect replica of a sprawling metropolis, a Tokyo or a São Paulo, engraved at atomic dimensions on a tile the size of a fingernail. The urban details would be faithfully rendered to the last golf ball or egg—each reduced to approximately the bulk of a hemoglobin molecule, or the distance grown by a human fingernail every five seconds. If a chip were merely a sculpture, this chiselling would represent a considerable achievement. But a chip is, in fact, a functional city for a population of busy electrons. They buzz about, flying our airplanes, powering the stock market, and, increasingly, thinking on our behalf. Unlike rockets, which are produced in relatively meagre quantities, microchips are stamped out by the billion. This is the most impressive thing about them. Or, maybe, about us.

blocks.html_en: Today, we very much care. Chips are the foundation of A.I., among other things, and A.I. is propping up our entire economy. The most valuable company in the world is the chip designer Nvidia. Last year, the company’s stock single-handedly accounted for about fifteen cents of every dollar returned by the S. & P. 500. From an economic perspective, the problem with chips nowadays is that there are never enough. A car might contain two thousand of them. When the pandemic caused supply-chain issues, automotive manufacturers found that they’d neglected to reserve a sufficient number. The government pressured chipmakers to reprioritize order fulfillment, safeguarding the birthright of Americans to buy new trucks. The chips that make Claude and ChatGPT talk are more specialized than those in a Chevy, and the chip industry has responded by reallocating its resources to these product lines. If basic chips grow scarce, it will not be long before the average homeowner cannot afford a dishwasher, let alone a phone. If the A.I. backlash seems fervent now, just wait until the dishes pile up.

Tech equities—for all intents and purposes, the stock market itself—wouldn’t be worth the paper they’re printed on. blocks.html_en: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or T.S.M.C., makes almost all of the world’s advanced chips, and has a market capitalization of around two trillion dollars. Of the ten most valuable companies globally, it is one of only two that are not American tech giants. (The other is Saudi Aramco.) Unlike T.S.M.C.’s peers—household names such as Apple, Google, and Amazon—the company has never cultivated much of a public-facing brand identity. Its fabs, as the factories are called, are only begrudgingly opened to clients, and even they are afforded a look only at their own production lines. The extreme reticence is by design. Some of the chip designs that the company executes, like those which animate an iPhone or a Mac, are inestimably precious trade secrets. Others, like the patterns for Nvidia’s top of the line, are treated like national-security assets, and are subject to American export controls.

blocks.html_en: T.S.M.C. is headquartered in the Hsinchu Science Park, a manicured enclave on the outskirts of a coastal city about an hour from Taipei. Its hulking fabs are neither hardened nor hidden. Some of them have panoramic views of white windmills, which dot the coastline of the Taiwan Strait like slender sentries. China lies a hundred miles or so over the water. The corporate nerve center is clad in the company palette of muted grays and bright-red accents. When I first approached the lobby, just before seven o’clock one humid morning in June, a maintenance man was showcasing the firm’s attention to detail. blocks.html_en: The origin story of Silicon Valley contains two contradictions. The first is about where it happened. One of its godfathers, Jack Kilby, was based not in California but in Dallas, at Texas Instruments. Silicon Valley was an idea, not a place. Fed up with Shockley’s managerial despotism, Noyce—along with seven colleagues, who became known as the Traitorous Eight—defected to found a rival firm, Fairchild Semiconductor, and then defected again to found Intel. In the ensuing decade, lawyers at Texas Instruments and at Fairchild fought a bitter court battle over the patent. blocks.html_en: The first integrated circuits on the market were compact, trustworthy, and completely unaffordable. The only plausible customer was the one organization with the desire and the budget to pursue an irrationally difficult goal at any cost: the federal government. For the nascent chipmakers, the military-industrial complex was a godsend. Aerospace and defense contracts paid for the capital-intensive installation of a manufacturing base. But executives chafed at the limitations of Washington’s monopsony: their engineers didn’t like answering to bureaucratic brass; sectors overreliant on government largesse get flabby; and only widespread demand would allow them to achieve economies of scale. The executives courted commercial interest, and this order volume translated into improved efficiency, accelerated research, and lowered prices. In 1971, Texas Instruments released the Pocketronic calculator. It offered four cutting-edge features: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. By the end of the decade, according to T. R. Reid’s “The Chip,” the United States had more calculators than people.

He’d noticed that, in each of the previous few years, transistor density—the number that could be shoehorned into the same footprint—had doubled. Moore casually reckoned that this trend would continue. At the time, a state-of-the-art chip had sixty transistors. By his logic, the chip of 1975 would accommodate sixty-five thousand—a ludicrous estimate. When the bet was settled, the newest chips boasted sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-six. If the automobile industry had innovated at the same pace, Moore calculated a few years later, “we would cruise comfortably in our cars at 100,000 mph, getting 50,000 miles per gallon of gasoline.” The wildest part is that the upgrades were essentially free. Moore went on, “We would find it cheaper to throw away our Rolls-Royce and replace it than to park it downtown for the evening.”

The actual machine has millions of parts and costs up to four hundred million dollars.

blocks.html_en: No single person can claim to comprehend an EUV machine in its entirety. The apparatus is roughly the size of two stacked fire trucks and is delivered to customers, such as T.S.M.C., in a fleet of seven 747s. When installed, it’s sheathed in cabinetry. A guide and I badged into one of a few dozen restricted cabins where the machine is assembled—an endeavor that takes about twenty weeks of round-the-clock work. The one before us was almost finished. Undressed, it had the appearance of a biomechanical hallucination: its monstrous exterior was trussed with a tangle of silver wires, cables, tubes, and dials, as if Optimus Prime had been put on life support. From a raised platform on the back side, a supervisor pointed to a small opening where some T.S.M.C. technician will begin the chip-printing process by feeding the machine an ingot of tin.

blocks.html_en: Tiny droplets of the molten tin are fired out of a cannon into a vacuum chamber, where they are shot—sixty thousand times a second—by unerring lasers. When the tin fog is ignited, the explosion produces a plasma fifty times hotter than the surface of the sun. The process, in other words, commences with the industrial production of miniature supernovas. These supernovas emit EUV that must be collected by Zeiss’s mirrors, which cannot function if their surface is marred by even a nanometre of tin debris. The only way to keep the mirrors pristine is to pump a continuous hurricane of hydrogen gas into the supernova’s blast radius. The gathered light ricochets through a hall of mirrors before it is bounced onto the blueprint of the chip. Making this happen a single time took decades of research. The profitability of ASML’s customers relies on it happening near-flawlessly twenty-four hours a day. Recurrent shutdowns, it’s not much of an exaggeration to say, would derail the global economy.

blocks.html_en: A few days before I arrived in Veldhoven, an internal event featured a conversation between ASML’s C.E.O., Christophe Fouquet, and Elon Musk. In the past, Musk has threatened to bypass any “rate limiter”—a “bottleneck” or “choke point” in chip production—with his own ingenuity. ASML is the sole purveyor of this particular tool, without which there are no advanced chips, and Musk was presumably referring to the fact that the company puts out only about fifty machines each year. He seems to regard the machines as overgrown photocopiers, and doesn’t understand why the company doesn’t make more faster. Musk isn’t the only kibbitzer who believes that a European firm, with its soft Continental indulgence of extended summer holidays, has taken the future hostage. This summer, after the embattled A.I.-finance guru Leopold Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund almost collapsed, he bravely coped by making a four-hundred-million-dollar investment in a U.S.-based lithography competitor. Frustrated American politicians, according to the Dutch journalist Marc Hijink, refer to ASML as “that company.”

blocks.html_en: The reason that nobody, in America or elsewhere, can “just” build an equivalent machine is that there’s no “just” about any of it. Some components are novel inventions. Others are transcendent renditions of existing products. A basic metal valve, for example, is available at any hardware store. The valves in ASML’s “droplet generator,” however, need to be able to handle molten metal under literally oceanic pressures, and to do so day and night for a year without wilting. The company had to find a supplier that could make such a valve. But venders didn’t have a financial incentive to do so, since ASML wouldn’t be buying the widget in normal widget quantities. ASML’s ability to persuade a vender anyway relied on an extended relationship, with accumulated reserves of trust on both sides. The basic model of competitive markets which one finds in an introductory economics textbook—where independent firms engage in cold arm’s-length transactions motivated by unadulterated self-interest—does not apply to the industry. It better resembles a kind of coöperative, or a planned economy.

blocks.html_en: A major module of the EUV machine is fashioned at an ASML facility in Connecticut that has the aura of an alchemist’s atelier. When I visited, in July, arcane prisms rotated on medieval-looking polishing machines. The facility hires the sorts of people who fix their own motorcycles. One young employee sat at a workbench in front of a block of milled amber glass that appeared extraterrestrial. The block, which bears a chip’s blueprint, levitates inside the machine. It moves with the precision necessary to trace a strand of DNA, even while enveloped in a robot that accelerates with forces great enough to tear an airliner apart nine times over. The entire apparatus is like an MRI machine that is expected to scan hairline fractures in the middle of a violent plane crash. The engineer proceeded by feel. He paused now and again to tap his fingers gently against a particular spot. It seemed less like engineering than like reflexology. This felt poignantly ironic. When you dig down to the very bedrock of A.I., you discover that underneath all of its cognitive power is a dude drumming his fingers with occult proficiency.

blocks.html_en: Just before 8 A.M. every day of the year, the gates of the Hsinchu Science Park are breached by a legion of commuters arriving on puttering scooters. T.S.M.C.’s home is lush and manicured, but it feels more like an autonomous zone than like a corporate complex. When I visited, this past summer, a guide pointed down the street to the National Experimental High School, from which his son would be graduating the next morning. We turned from Prosperity Road 1 onto Prosperity Road 2. Expert launderers of clean-room bunny suits careened by in branded wagons. There are administrative pavilions, post offices, banks, clinics, and two universities. Some employees live in dorms on site, and all of them have easy access to pools and fitness centers. You rarely have to walk more than a block to visit a sparkling 7-Eleven. T.S.M.C.’s suppliers—tooling companies such as Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron, as well as software firms such as Cadence and Synopsys—maintain their own local embassies.

blocks.html_en: The visionary behind this vibrant terrarium is Morris Chang. Born in 1931 in the Chinese city of Ningbo, he was raised in wartime flight—moving from Nanjing to Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Chongqing, Shanghai—and resolved to find peace at a university overseas. He enrolled at Harvard, planning to study Shakespeare, but quickly realized that engineering was a more secure path for Asian immigrants, and transferred to M.I.T. At twenty-seven, he accepted a job at Texas Instruments, just in time for the invention of the integrated circuit. Chang was tasked with the problem of yield, or the percentage of finished transistors that worked. The production line that he was given had a yield of approximately zero. With his pipe in his mouth, Chang devoted himself to operational excellence. Within a few months, the yield exceeded twenty per cent.

blocks.html_en: The postwar Taiwanese economy churned out low-margin goods, such as umbrellas and toys, for foreign clients. Mattel didn’t need domestic Barbie factories if a Taiwanese partner could produce dolls more cheaply. Such factories could also then amortize their fixed costs by making adjacent products for other brands. Chang proposed a semiconductor “foundry,” which would do for pricey chips what its predecessors had done for cheap junk. At the time, however, the market didn’t exist. Chipmakers had plenty of overseas help—in the book “Chip War,” the scholar Chris Miller notes they were globalizing long before the word gained currency—but the industry was also known for vertical integration, and did the hardest parts in-house. “Morris, you’ve had a lot of good ideas in your time,” Gordon Moore told Chang. “This isn’t one of them.” Jerry Sanders, the C.E.O. of the American chip company A.M.D., had once notoriously declared that “real men have fabs.”

blocks.html_en: Real men, as it happened, are delighted not to have to spend twenty billion dollars on a fab. By the end of T.S.M.C.’s first decade, the company was bringing in a billion dollars in annual revenue. In 1993, a young Taiwanese American named Jensen Huang had an idea for a specialized graphics chip, or G.P.U., to intensify the video-game experience, and founded Nvidia. It wasn’t long before design mishaps drove Nvidia to the brink of bankruptcy. Huang sent a personal letter to Chang, and got a call at his office a week later. (The story, in Stephen Witt’s “The Thinking Machine,” is that Huang yelled, “Everybody shut the fuck up—I’ve got Morris Chang on the phone.”) T.S.M.C. took a chance on his prototype. The specialized architecture of Nvidia’s chips turned out to be ideally suited to the development of A.I. In the meantime, Apple developed a novel chip for mobile devices and eventually asked T.S.M.C. to make it. The result was every generation of iPhone that has been produced since 2014.

blocks.html_en: T.S.M.C. has come to embody national strength and national purpose. A shy, cerebral engineer named Nicholas Lee translates abstract research into procedures that can survive implementation on the factory floor. A machine might need to be tuned, for example, to compensate for low air pressure from an incoming typhoon. He joined T.S.M.C. four years ago, right out of a master’s program in chemical engineering at the preëminent National Taiwan University. When I asked how many of his classmates had done the same, he laughed and said, “At least sixty per cent.” He added, “Everyone thinks there’s something wrong with you if you don’t accept a T.S.M.C. job.” To enlist at T.S.M.C. is to give one’s parents the gift of familial honor. The company’s lower echelons, which tend to be populated by graduates of vocational or technical schools that serve as T.S.M.C. feeders, have the same social coherence. Although it’s a “very intense work environment,” the challenges were eased by the fact that, as Lee told me, “we all grew up together.” One in forty-six babies in Taiwan is born to a T.S.M.C. employee.

It is coated with an ultrathin film of glass or metal, glazed with photosensitive chemicals, and then passed through a lithography machine. The chemicals are rinsed off, and the pattern on the exposed film is etched in relief by blasts of plasma before being gassed with other chemicals. The wafer is washed, polished, and inspected for flaws. For the most advanced chips, this gantlet is then repeated about a hundred times on a loop, as if an entire city skyline were being raised one story at a time.

blocks.html_en: AP6, which opened in 2023, was T.S.M.C.’s first fab devoted to the entire process of “advanced packaging,” an innovation at the cutting edge of the industry. Advanced packaging interlaces several individual chips to form a composite superchip. The challenge is that chips are carved in the miniature realm where matter itself has the irregularity of wood grain. blocks.html_en: I met Renee Tseng, a young woman in casually elegant denim, who was part of the first wave of Taiwanese employees sent to set up the Arizona operations. Hopefully, in time, her American counterparts would get their reps in.

blocks.html_en: The catch, in the American attempt to make chips at home rather than overseas, is that chips aren’t really made anywhere at all. A chip can cross international borders more than seventy times before it’s shipped to a customer. T.S.M.C.’s part begins with silicon wafers, but these have their own far-flung prehistory. Leading-edge semiconductor-grade polysilicon must be purified to “eleven nines” (99.999999999 per cent), which only a handful of specialized companies—based in Michigan, Germany, and Japan—are poised to do. These silicon chunks are melted in bespoke crucibles made of the world’s purest quartz, virtually all of which is mined from a solitary deposit in the mountains of North Carolina. This process, which generates perfectly crystalline silicon ingots to be sliced like fragile metallic salamis into thin wafers, is entrusted largely to one firm in Taiwan and two in Japan. Most of the steps along this chain are controlled by monopolies or duopolies. This isn’t because of market manipulation. It’s because each endeavor is so esoteric, so formidable, and so crucial that it makes sense for all the available expertise to be concentrated in one or two nexuses.

The first point they want to make is always the same; as Dylan Patel, who runs the research-and-consulting firm SemiAnalysis, told me, “The main thing people don’t understand is that semiconductors are the most complicated things people do.” The second point they make, before there is time to articulate an objection, is that everyone’s intuitive response is incorrect. Patel continued, “Rockets are simple.” Brinton Johns, an investor at N.Z.S. Capital, said, of making chips, “It’s just so much harder. Rockets are an amazing accomplishment, yes. We don’t have a rating scale for complexity, but rockets are maybe a five or a six.” His investing partner, Jon Bathgate, finished the thought: “Semiconductors are an eleven.”

blocks.html_en: In its most spiritual version, Moore’s Law projected that our power would routinely double. But this idea was not original to Gordon Moore. It was Henry Adams, in 1904, who first proposed what he called the Law of Acceleration. The world’s output of coal, he’d noticed, had roughly doubled each decade since 1840. Should this rate hold, he imagined, an American in the year 2000 would have “unlimited” power and “think in complexities unimaginable to an earlier mind.” He’d been famously converted by an experience at the Paris Exposition’s great gallery of machines, where he perceived the towering inventions “as a moral force, much as the early Christians felt the Cross.” This devotion had sustained the generations who built the great cathedral at Chartres. What they had accomplished in the name of the Virgin was now accomplished in the name of the Dynamo. But what Adams took as objects of devotion might better be described as occasions for it. They have given vast numbers of individual people, largely unknown to one another, reason to collaborate on a project that they would not live to see completed.

blocks.html_en: Last year, I happened to be talking to a Dutch archeologist, Maikel Kuijpers, about Neolithic monuments. Stonehenge, he said, has frequently been investigated as a technological mystery. We look at the enormous rock slabs retrieved from far-off sites by archaic peoples and can’t help but suspect that these ancients availed themselves of some precocious technology lost to history—a present from aliens, perhaps. But we know how they built it, Kuijpers went on. There isn’t any mystery. They gathered as many people and animals as they could, and distributed ropes, and together they hauled those tremendous slabs a great distance. This didn’t diminish their achievement. It made it, if anything, even more sublime. ♦
